name: Gua sha stone

lead: Gua sha is a traditional East Asian technique in which a smooth-edged tool is stroked over lubricated skin. The facial version, using jade or rose quartz stones, is used to de-puff and sculpt the jaw and cheeks and for a lymphatic-drainage style massage.

The pressure and stroking temporarily increase blood flow and move fluid, easing puffiness for a time. Trials of body gua sha mostly examine pain; research on facial use is sparse, including a 2025 randomized trial in 34 women comparing facial roller and gua sha massage over 8 weeks on contour, muscle tone and elasticity.

paras: Users glide the stone along the neck, jaw, cheeks and brow with oil or serum for a few minutes, usually in the morning or before events. Stones sell for roughly $10 to $25. The de-puffing look is generally described as lasting hours.

Facial use is low risk, though pressing too hard can bruise. Traditional body gua sha intentionally raises red marks. Evidence for lasting changes to facial structure is limited, and the effect is described as temporary.

angle.text: Stroking the face with a stone moves fluid out of the jaw and cheeks, giving a de-puffed, more sculpted look that lasts hours. A 2025 trial compared facial roller and gua sha massage over 8 weeks.

lead: Gua sha is a traditional East Asian technique in which a smooth-edged tool is pressed and stroked over lubricated skin. In its traditional form, applied to the body for pain, colds and fatigue, it is performed until red or purple petechiae, known as sha, appear [1]. A gentler facial version, using stones such as jade or rose quartz, has become popular in skincare, where it is promoted for contouring, de-puffing and lymphatic drainage [1].

The facial and traditional uses have different evidence bases. Trials of body gua sha have mostly examined pain conditions such as neck and low back pain, and a 2018 meta-analysis of gua sha trials in perimenopausal syndrome found most to be of low methodological quality [2][3][4]. Research on cosmetic facial use is sparse: a 2025 randomized trial in 34 women compared facial roller and gua sha massage over 8 weeks on facial contour, muscle tone and skin elasticity [5], and a 2023 dermatology letter discussed whether gua sha, jade rollers and facial massage offer benefits [6].

Wikipedia characterises traditional gua sha as a pseudoscientific practice that lacks high-quality evidence of clinical benefit and notes that it nearly always causes minor skin trauma [1]. Practitioners and traditional medicine texts describe it as releasing stagnation of qi and blood [1]. Facial stones are sold at roughly $10 to $25.

paras: The name comes from the Chinese gua, to scrape, and sha, the petechial marks that appear on the skin afterwards. In traditional Chinese medicine sha is associated with stagnation of qi and blood that the practice aims to release [1]. English-language names include spooning and coining, and the French term tribo-effleurage [1].

Tools include ceramic spoons, coins, jade stones and water buffalo horn, used with massage oil or balm along muscle groups or meridians [1]. Pressure is described as lighter for cosmetic purposes such as facial gua sha and firmer for musculoskeletal complaints [1]. Facial gua sha stones are generally flat, shaped tools with curved edges designed to follow the contours of the jaw, cheek and brow.

Wikipedia traces the practice to ancient China and says it was formalised in traditional medicine during the Ming dynasty (1368-1644), when texts documented it for sha syndromes attributed to environmental factors such as wind or cold [1]. An AI-generated encyclopedia summary lists earlier references in texts from the Jin, Tang and Song periods and monographs from the Qing dynasty, but this account is from an untrusted secondary source [7].

The practice remains a common home remedy in Vietnamese, Cambodian and Indonesian communities, where it has other local names. In the 1980s, sha marks on children were sometimes mistaken by Western clinicians for signs of abuse, which produced misunderstandings and distrust of providers; the 2001 Hong Kong film The Gua Sha Treatment dramatises such a case [1]. Gua sha surged on TikTok in 2021 and 2022, driven by beauty influencers promoting the facial version for lymphatic drainage and skin rejuvenation [1].

Gua sha is a common home remedy in Vietnamese, Cambodian and Indonesian communities, and Wikipedia reports that in the 1980s some Vietnamese immigrants in the United States feared child-abuse reports after using the practice (cao gio) on children, because the marks can be misread as signs of abuse. The 2001 Hong Kong film The Gua Sha Treatment dramatises such a case.[1] A 2018 JAMA Dermatology article on gua sha, also called coining therapy, addresses the marks it leaves.[8]

The way the practice is described is itself disputed. Wikipedia calls traditional gua sha pseudoscientific and notes a lack of high-quality evidence of benefit, while practitioners and traditional medicine texts describe it as releasing stagnation of qi and blood, and a 2021 review in the Journal of Family Medicine and Primary Care surveys contemporary views on scraping therapy.[1][4] Some US states include it within traditional Chinese medicine licensing, according to Wikipedia.[1]

In traditional medicine, scraping is believed to clear stagnation and promote circulation of blood and qi [1]. A 2007 pilot study in healthy subjects, the first on the physiology of gua sha, examined its effects on microcirculation of skin and subcutaneous tissue, with the aim of understanding mechanisms for the observed pain relief [9][10]. A 2012 study measured effects of scraping on local temperature and blood perfusion in healthy subjects [11]. Reviews of reflex therapies including gua sha propose effects on nociceptors and spinal pain pathways and a possible role for relaxation [12].

The 2012 study used a within-person design in 23 healthy adults aged 20 to 40: the right back was scraped for 5 minutes with a buffalo horn tool and lubricant, and the left side served as a comparison. Laser Doppler imaging showed blood perfusion in the scraped area roughly doubling immediately afterwards and remaining above the unscraped side at 90 minutes, while the area was about 1 degree Celsius warmer for around an hour. All participants reported warmth and slight pain and showed redness with small subcutaneous bloody spots.[11] These measurements were on the back with firm scraping, not on the face with light strokes.
For facial use, proponents describe stroking as moving fluid and increasing local circulation, which may transiently reduce puffiness. No study has measured lymphatic flow after facial gua sha.

A 2010 systematic review of controlled trials examined gua sha for musculoskeletal pain [2], and a 2015 meta-analysis of traditional Chinese medicine for neck and low back pain is among the larger pooled analyses touching related therapies [13]. A 2018 meta-analysis of six randomized trials of gua sha for perimenopausal syndrome found that most trials were of low methodological quality [3].

The 2010 systematic review searched 11 databases to July 2009 and identified 7 controlled trials of gua sha for musculoskeletal pain (5 randomised), all conducted in China with 60 to 240 participants. Two found gua sha better than acupuncture; the others found no significant difference, and all seven were rated at high risk of bias. The reviewers concluded that the evidence was insufficient to show effectiveness for pain and called for better-designed trials, and no adverse events were reported in the included studies.[2]
For cosmetic facial use, evidence is limited to small trials and commentary [5][6].

Facial: a 2025 randomized comparative trial assigned 34 women aged 20 to 50 to facial roller or gua sha massage for 10 minutes, five times per week for 8 weeks, with outcome measures covering facial contour, muscle tone and skin elasticity [5].

Pain: a randomized trial of 50 people with chronic low back pain compared two gua sha treatments with a waitlist control, using pain intensity as the primary outcome [14]. A randomized trial of gua sha in chronic neck pain [15] and a randomized pilot study of neck and low back pain [16] were also published, as was a 2025 randomized trial examining thoracolumbar fascia thickness in low back pain [17].

Other conditions: randomized trials have examined gua sha in breast engorgement [18], Parkinson's disease pain [19] and Parkinson's disease with REM sleep behavior disorder [20]. A Cochrane review of treatments for breast engorgement found little evidence of an effective intervention among the approaches studied [21]. A 2024 guideline-mapping review looked at traditional Chinese medicine recommendations for insomnia [22].
A 2018 JAMA Dermatology article addresses gua sha, also called coining therapy [8].

Facial gua sha uses a flat stone with curved edges, typically jade, rose quartz or similar, stroked over oil or serum along the neck, jaw, cheek and brow. Wikipedia notes that pressure is lighter for facial use than for musculoskeletal complaints, and that the practice's surge on TikTok in 2021 and 2022 was driven by beauty influencers promoting lymphatic drainage and skin rejuvenation.[1] Users describe a routine of a few minutes, often paired with moisturiser or facial oil, aimed at a sharper jawline, less morning puffiness and a healthy flush.

Promoters say stroking toward the lymph nodes moves fluid and tension out of the face, and that the massage relaxes muscles around the jaw and forehead. A 2023 dermatology letter asks whether gua sha, jade rollers and facial massage have benefits within dermatology, and the 2025 randomised trial of 34 women compared a roller and gua sha for contour, muscle tone and elasticity over eight weeks.[5][6] Researchers have measured skin blood flow and temperature after body scraping, which gives a physiological basis for the temporary flush people notice.[9][11]

Traditional body gua sha intentionally raises petechiae and nearly always causes some skin trauma such as redness or bruising. Reported adverse effects range from dermatitis, burns and blood in the urine to rare severe events including bleeding in the brain and injuries requiring skin grafts [1]. Infection is a concern when tools are not sterilised or skin is broken, and Wikipedia notes no documented blood-borne transmission directly linked to gua sha [1]. Published safety protocols for gua sha and cupping address precautions [23].
Facial technique is generally lighter. Pressing too hard can still bruise.

Facial gua sha is discussed as a massage step for jawline definition and de-puffing, in looksmaxxing spaces that focus on facial bloat and soft-tissue appearance. A looksmax.org guide framed around getting a 'more chiselled face' lists benefits such as circulation, lymphatic drainage, reduced puffiness, fewer fine lines and release of muscle tension, and replies range from a user who says it helped them to one who says the promotional video exists to sell the tool.[24] In a separate thread on whether a purpose-made tool can be replaced, members discuss substitutes and cleaning.[25]

The appeal described in these threads is that the tool is inexpensive and used as part of a skincare routine alongside oils or serums. Users generally describe the effects as short-lived, such as a flush and reduced morning puffiness, rather than a lasting change to bone or fat structure.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, facial gua sha is discussed as a tool for a leaner, less bloated face, and some users question whether it is worth buying; posts often borrow benefit lists from traditional descriptions of the practice [25][24].
